utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution would wish to raise two short preliminary matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Your Honours, last Friday, the Chamber entered its decision on the Prosecution's 27th Rule 92 bis motion. The Chamber admitted RM054's closed session testimony in Kvocka and one associated exhibit without designating them to be admitted under seal. We believe this may have been an oversight and would ask the Chamber to investigate and consider amending its decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll seriously consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The second matter, Your Honour, in response to the Trial Chamber's request to be notified regarding translations of the documents on our 11th motion to amend Rule 65 ter exhibit list dated the 2nd of August, 2013, the Prosecution now confirms that all English translations have been received and uploaded into e-court for all 993 documents. These have been assigned 65 ter numbers 29171 through 30163. And that's all I wanted to say, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this update, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, there's one other very brief matter. Yesterday I sent an e-mail regarding the scheduling problem next week. In discussing the matter with Mr. Lukic this morning, he believes that can he accomplish all he needs to in six hours, so the scheduling problem is no longer relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, of course, the parties should be very disciplined in sticking strictly to the estimates. But that then resolved the matter I wanted to put on the record; that is, whether we would sit either two hours somewhere during the week or to have a short session on Wednesday. But we leave it, as matters stand now, to the parties. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Yes, and, as a matter of fact, I can quickly respond, Mr. Groome, about the status of the documents admitted in the 27th Rule 92 bis decision. Because, on the 8th of November, in its decision on the Prosecution's 27th motion to admit evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis, the Chamber admitted into evidence in relation to RM054 excerpts of the witness's testimony from Prosecutor versus Kvocka and -- et al and the document bearing Rule 65 ter number 13888. These documents should have been admitted under seal, and therefore the Chamber instructs the Registry to change their status to under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dannatt.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic will now continue his cross-examination. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to take up where we left off yesterday, the Krstic trial and your book.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could have in e-court 1D1448, page 17. This ought to correspond to pages 260 and 261 of the book. And I would like to focus on the left at about three-quarters of the way down on the page. And it begins: "During the trial it become very apparent that his principal failing had been a personal moral one. His body language in the dock increasingly indicated that he knew that his principal mistake was in blindly accepting the order given to him directly by Ratko Mladic on 12 July 1995 to instruct his troops to conduct mass killings."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, here, you again seem to reference an explicit order given directly to Krstic from Ratko Mladic on 12 July 1995. Can you please confirm for us that this conclusion by you is not based on any physical orders that you saw from General Mladic ordering any kind of massacre?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's correct. It's my assumption on the basis that, within the chain of command that was operating, the one person that could give an instruction to General Krstic was General Mladic. And my personal observation during the course of the Krstic trial was that General Krstic had done something that he was most uncomfortable to do and had done so as a result of following instructions from another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is your assumption also based upon your review of Richard Butler's report entitled: "The Srebrenica Narrative"?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I would stay with what I wrote in my book. It was my observation over an extended period of time giving evidence and watching the effect of that evidence in examination and cross-examination on the demeanour of General Krstic who, to my observation, and it's my opinion, had begun with giving me the impression of a confident, professional military man, but when confronted by the material that was put to him during the course of the time that I was giving evidence, seemed to look increasingly uncomfortable. And I drew the deduction that there was a realisation that he knew that he had done wrong. And as I have just said, the only person who could have given him instructions was his military superior, which we know in the chain of command was General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So did you not have this conclusion or predisposition against General Mladic before you were an expert in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I felt it my duty to come to a conclusion about anyone's guilt. I appeared in this court 13, 14 years ago in order to give my opinions on a range of matters for the benefit of the Court. I did not feel then or now it's my duty in court to express an opinion on anyone's guilt or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dannatt, the question simply was whether you had this conclusion before you were an expert. That's a factual question. Whether it was your duty or not to develop any opinion is a different matter. Did you have that opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have that opinion, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 12 of your book in e-court which should correlate to pages 224 to 225 of the book, and if we can focus on the middle paragraph of the page that is on the right-hand side: "But not everyone believed [sic] so" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "Behaved so."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "... behaved so. The following Sunday, Sky TV released an interview with Radovan Karadzic in which he taunted NATO for its inability to arrest him and indeed asserted that it would be stupid of us to try. I looked on with interest, knowing that he would not be able to run forever, but having no idea that he would elude capture for so long. I had been given orders that if he did come into the Banja Luka area he should be detained. Such an arrest would undoubtedly have been another major bump on the path to peace, but I thought that it would certainly be very worthwhile. Privately, though, I believed that arresting General Ratko Mladic was quite another matter. The Bosnian Serb army was very loyal to him and an arrest at that time could have had a very violent backlash, one that was not worth the risk given the sensitive process in which we were then immersed. Like Karadzic, this monster could not run forever. One day justice would apprehend him."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm for us whether your views of General Mladic being a monster date from the time-period when you were in Banja Luka in 1995?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you still hold these same views of General Mladic that he is monster and that you desire him to be apprehended by justice?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can now turn to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which is P2629, marked for identification. Paragraph 27 of the same, which would be page 7 in the English, page 6 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here, sir, you describe how the British Army has changed from centrally controlled to this manoeuvrist approach. Does that mean that it is common for an army's doctrine to change in order to address the present factual circumstances facing a nation?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over time, it is possible to do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did your extensive research and experience reveal if the Yugoslavian military, that is, the JNA, or the Yugoslav defence doctrine change at all or were they static and unchanging from their inception until the dissolution of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The model of a centralised command and control system, I believe, remained in places throughout the lifetime of the JNA and of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's only now that the interpreters have finished their interpretation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, do you consider the British approach to mission command doctrine to be demonstrative of other NATO nations and their armies?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is demonstrative of those that are predominantly volunteer armies, which I would include the United States. And over the last ten years a number of European armies that previously relied heavily on conscripts have become increasingly made up of volunteers, and as their level of training and education has increased, they are moving more towards the NATO model, which is a model based on the manoeuvrist approach, mission command and Auftragstaktik which lends itself to armies that are professional as opposed to conscript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to now take a look at 1D1449. I can introduce that as being an article dating from 2009 in the Canadian Military Journal by a Keith Stewart. And I'd like to look together at the bottom of the first column of the first page. Start: "Information age scholars Donald S. Alberts and Richard E. Hayes have proposed a spectrum of command and control approaches in which they distinguish between 'order specific,' 'objective specific' and 'mission specific' philosophies. These discussions have focused upon the levels of control centralisation and directive specificity in orders. 'Order specific' approaches tend to be adopted by command organisations that maintain centralised control and issue regular, detailed orders. The Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) and former Soviet armies are cited as examples. 'Mission specific' approaches are at the opposite end of the scale and describe low levels of central control such as employed by the Israeli Army and by the German Army during the Second World War. The centre of the spectrum is occupied by 'objective specific' approaches." Sir, do you agree, based upon your expertise, with what is written here about there being a spectrum of command and control approaches --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Again, it is only now that the interpreters were able to finish their interpretation. Could we all slow down. Could you answer the question, Mr. Dannatt.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you read with us whether you -- your question was complete already?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was. Could you then answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a second time, I say yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I missed it the first time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can return to the text and the next paragraph, which will bleed onto the next page: "Within this category, Alberts and Hayes contrast 'problem bounding' and 'problem solving' approaches. The former, they suggest, is consistent with British doctrine, and it is speculated here that it is broadly equivalent to the" - and if we can go to the next page. Again it will be the left-hand side - "approaches adopted in the Canadian and Australian armies. Alberts and Hayes observe that although British headquarters provide directives based upon objectives to be accomplished, they tend to present them in very general terms. They propose that 'problem bounding' directives are less detailed than those issued by commanders in 'problem solving' environments - 'often by a factor of three to one, reflecting this lack of detail.' By contrast, problem solving approaches are characterised by a tendency to provide more substantial guidance as to how objectives are to be met. Alberts and Hayes suggest that it is this approach that has been adopted by the US Army since the Second World War." General, do you agree with what is presented here?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Alberts' and Hayes' opinion. I read it with interest. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I take that as a disagreement then, sir.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can't. I think it's an interesting comment. I think it's a very general comment to sweep up into one sentence an operational approach said to be adopted by the US Army since the Second World War. In that 60- or 70-year period, the US Army has gone through several transformations based on experiences in places such as Vietnam, and their approach to command and control, their approach to training, equipment and discipline has changed more than once over that extended period of time. So I say again, I note Alberts' and Hayes' opinion. I don't necessarily share it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could take a look at the next paragraph that begins "differences." I'd like to skip to the middle of that paragraph where it starts talking: "A high-profile example ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like for you to follow along as we introduce that part: "A high-profile example of this difference in command philosophy resulting in friction is provided by the American General Wesley Clark, who believes that it was a major contributing factor to his well-publicised disagreement with the British KFOR commander, Lieutenant-General Sir Michael Jackson, during the Kosovo campaign. Clark reflected that 'in the British system, a field commander is given mission-type orders, not detailed and continuing guidance ... the American military has always aspired to this model, but has seldom seemed to attain it.' Likewise, in his now notorious assessment of the US Army's early experience in Iraq, the British Brigadier, Aylwin-Foster, states, 'that commanders and staff at all levels were reluctant to deviate from precise instructions.' This raises another interesting issue. Although it is one that cannot be developed further here: namely, that as well as representing a 'top-down' managerial approach, a culture of command by detailed orders is also 'demand-driven.' That is, unless they are carefully trained otherwise, personnel will expect and prefer to receive detailed direction - especially in high-risk situations." And I'd end there and ask you, sir, since you -- I -- I believe you have personal knowledge of General Clark and General Jackson's experiences in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with the differences between the British and the US doctrine as described by General Clark, on the one hand, and by Brigadier Aylwin-Foster on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think their opinions interesting, and not far removed from reality. As the quote said, the US aspire to mission command, but in a very large army, they have not always been able to deploy it, have not always been able to follow it in the way that they would like to. And Brigadier Aylwin-Foster's comments are interesting and they were controversial at the time, and they caused a bit of trouble at the time, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to turn to the JNA. If we can go to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: P2629, marked for identification, at page 6 in the English and page 5 of the B/C/S, paragraph 24 is what I would like to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here, sir, you talk about the antecedents for the VRS being in the JNA and that the doctrinal roots of both are in the Soviet model. In this paragraph and the next one of your statement, you cite several JNA publications from the early 1990s. Do you consider that these publications are fully representative of the entirety of the origins and the doctrinal roots of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they are a sufficient basis on which the VRS was founded from the doctrinal -- received doctrinal understanding of the JNA, bearing in mind that many of the officers and leaders of the VRS had former service in the JNA and therefore had been educated and trained by the method of command and control practiced by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For purposes of your research and review, did you ever come across the name of Dr. James Gow from the King's College in London and someone who has testified for the Prosecution as an expert in other proceedings such as the Celebici case?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of James Gow. I don't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can please have 1D1446 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it -- Mr. Ivetic, is it Gall or is it Gow?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Gow, G-o-w, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer related to Dr. James Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we see one of Dr. Gow's publications or books on the screen. This is something that we received from the Prosecution in disclosure. Have you had occasion to ever review this book and read it?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not read that book, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd propose to take a look at some of the things that are said about the origins of the Yugoslav military.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to page 40 of this document in e-court, page 33 of the book, and it will be starting with the last sentence on this page and will then bleed then on over to the next page dealing with December 1941. And I begin: "The next major step came in December, when the 1st Proletarian" -- I apologise. And then if we go, yeah: "... Shock Brigade was formed. By the end of the war, there had been 295 brigades. These were elite units, service in them was the highest honour for every individual fighting man - specifically under Communist leadership which could operate wherever necessary. Thus, while retaining a national, or territorial character (in the main), these were the first formations of an army that could be directed from the centre to perform tasks anywhere. "Prior to this, the military effort depended on local feelings but this led to low reliability. For instance, Djilas describes how Montenegrin peasants, who had been quick to rise up and take action, abandoned the cause once the Italians mounted an offensive: 'To escape artillery fire, they had abandoned the position. The peasants sped back to their homes, hoping to save their families and animals, and no force on earth could have stopped them.' The territorial specificity of the early partisan detachments meant not only that members might fight only for their own village, but that they were in constant touch with their households, frequently sleeping there. This kind of attachment had awkward consequences, especially if an individual was killed. To avoid these situations and create a less territorially defined, more flexible military structure, brigades were introduced."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'll stop right there and ask you, sir, was this something that you came across in your research, the earlier territorial-based units and the switch to brigades in 1941?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is very interesting comment on the early days of what became the JNA, and I note, with interest, the earlier part of the quotation that you read out. That brigades, and I quote now, "were the first formation of an army that could be directed from the centre to perform tasks anywhere." What that tells me is that the realisation that leaving it just to the man on a the ground to do whatever he thought was right was not going to be militarily effective, as the rest of your quote would indicate, and that therefore there was a need to have better trained, more centrally controlled units which could carry out their tasks as required in a better fashion. I find that very interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could scroll down not to the next paragraph but the one thereafter, I'd like to continue the talk of the brigades. Dr. Gow's book reads as follows: "The brigades' greatest attraction was mobility. The concept of mobile territorial units was, to some extent, an inheritance of the former Royal Army's thinking, a product of the incorporation of some of that army's officers in the new movement. It was also a descendant of the Serbian forces in the First Balkan War."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did your research into the doctrinal roots of the JNA include research of the Royal Yugoslav Army and the Serbian forces in the First Balkan War?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But thank you for drawing my attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 47 in e-court. And this will be page 40 of the underlying book.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to direct your attention to the first paragraph under the heading: "Military legitimacy in the post-war period: The functional imperative." And it reads as follows: "Taking military doctrine as the imperative of functional legitimacy, the post-war evolution of the YPA (including the change from the Yugoslav Army to the Yugoslav People's Army) falls into three phases. In the first, the YPA was established as a conventional standing army. In the second, the army returned to its partisan roots, becoming a territorial militia army. In the final period, the army no longer encompassed the territorial aspect of defence; instead, it became one element in a duplex defence system, the two structures being an operational army and a territorial defence force. "Official versions of the post-war development of the armed forces give the dates for the three stages as follows: 1945 to 1958; 1958 to 1968, and 1969 onwards. These are the dates when new military doctrines were formally adapted on the basis of new defence laws. However, if account is taken of the three factors said to define military doctrine, a different picture emerges." In the course of your research and work on preparing your expert statement on the origins of the JNA and the VRS, did you, in fact, come across information about these changes in military doctrine by the Yugoslav forces?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I would comment, and I repeat a comment as I made yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Please continue, General.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would repeat a comment that I made yesterday, that sometimes loose language is used in military discussions, and the three phases of development of, let's call the JNA, actually represent the following of three strategies as opposed to doctrines. I say again what I said yesterday, a doctrine indicates how an army thinks. A strategy is the headline of what it does. And what you have just described to me that I'm sufficiently familiar with is three stages of development when the strategies, the national strategies of Yugoslavia, changed. And they describe that very accurately. Thank you for drawing that interesting passage to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I briefly consult with my ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the interpretation has finished now, you may briefly consult with your client. But usual conditions: Short and whispering rather than audible speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Mladic, would you please return to your initial volume. Mr. Ivetic, could you ask Mr. Mladic to return to his initial volume. Mr. -- Mr. Mladic, I stop you now. I will not allow any further consultations if Mr. Mladic does not speak at low volume. Then he has to wait until the next break, which is in 15 minutes from now, and then you can take instructions during that break, Mr. Ivetic, and you can put whatever questions you wish after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 44 -- page 51 of the document in e-court, which should be page 44 ... I apologise. Next page. Last paragraph of the page, and it will bleed over onto the next page, talking about the restructuring of the Yugoslav military: "Before long, there was another new military doctrine and concomitant re-organisation. General People's Defence (GPD) came into force in 1969. The Yugoslav armed forces were to get a radically different structure. Territorial Defence was emphasised by a division of responsibility. Until this point and in other instances of armed," if can you go to the next page, "forces based on a territorial principle, sole responsibility for defence had been with the central institution of defence; usually, territorial forces have been integrated with, or adjunct to the army. GPD divided responsibility between the YPA and socio-political communities. "According to the 1969 National Defence Law, the Yugoslav armed forces would comprise two equal elements: The YPA and Territorial Defence. Whereas the YPA would be the responsibility of the federal authorities, Territorial Defence would be organised by socio-political communities, that is, republics, autonomous provinces, communes and work organisations."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can end there, I think, and I'll ask you again: Do you stand by your testimony that the changes in the Yugoslav military doctrine relate only to strategy and do not relate to command and control, based upon what we've just read here?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what we've just read there is a very clear description of a shift in national strategic stance, one that I completely recognise, and the way Territorial Defence is described and organised is something that one recognises throughout the latter history of Yugoslavia and into the way, in many ways, that the part of Bosnia that was controlled by the Serbs operated. Local defence is very much part and parcel of the organisation. That was a strategic shift. It's -- doesn't actually have that much bearing of the doctrine of military command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page, which should be page 47 of the underlying book, the last two paragraphs on the page: "As in earlier periods, however, much of the doctrine was theoretically compatible with self-management and thus was a welcome but secondary feature. If 1967 offered a ten-year perspective on the armed forces' progress that would indicated -- that which indicated a continuing need to work intensively on the optimal solution to problems in that quarter was not the need to produce a more social form of defence. Although, in practice, GPD met civilian demands for self-managing principles to be applied to the armed forces, bringing defence into line with the decentralising confederative tendencies of society at that time, the changes did not owe anything to the theoretical argument. "The 1969 changes constituted a diminishing of the YPA's institutional status, where previously it had sole and virtually unquestioned authority in defence matters, it had been reduced to a co-equal." And then if we could turn to two paragraphs down from here. A little more. Should begin: "War-time experiences ..." Up a little bit. Just missed it. There we go: "War-time experience had shown that small units operating locally could not be centrally commanded. Were Yugoslavia to be attacked, it would have been highly unlikely that the YPA could achieve full mobilisation before certain areas were occupied by the enemy; certainly it could not have provided anything more than specialist local leadership in the event of territory being seized."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, does this that we've just gone through comprise your understanding of the system that was introduced subsequent to 1969 in Yugoslavia in relation to the Yugoslav army and the Territorial Defence system?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise that. And it is an interesting description of one part of the development of what was going on in the former Yugoslavia. I have to question, however, in my own mind, the relevance to -- between that and the situation of the Bosnian Serb Army between 1992 and 1995. Different conflicts at different points in history, and I stand by the centralised nature of the VRS. But thank you for bringing this to my attention. I found it very interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you give us your understanding of the changes that were being instituted in 1988 in the Yugoslav army according to your research and expertise, sir?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't go into that. Thank you. I can't answer that question. Perhaps you'd like to tell me. You've been very instructive so far this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 66 of the book in e-court. And if we could focus on the middle paragraph of the page that starts: "It is not clear why that tradition was ended ..." And I would start with the line right there, three lines from the top on the screen: "Already in 1974, the co-equality" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, please sit down. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "Already by 1974, the co-equality of the two elements of the armed forces in the five-year-old GPD system had become imbalanced, the YPA, de facto, having become the senior element. Gradual erosion of regional authority in the Territorial Defence Force (TDF) was completed in 1980 with the establishment of a Council for Territorial Defence. Answerable only to the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, which was staffed by soldiers, and of which the minister was always the most senior YPA officer, the council's foundation meant a concentration of the [sic] YPA control; the TDF became an integral part of the YPA itself. Creeping centralisation within the YPA culminating with the changes which included the LAD's abolition was signalled by the end of 1987. At that time, the ZMD, which assumed the responsibilities of the LAD and its equivalent in Zagreb, was formed. The year 1988 would appear to have been one of transition." Does this accord with your knowledge of the facts and the changes being undergone by the Yugoslav military in 1988, just a few years before the dissolution of that army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in very general terms, I would recognise that. But if I'm allowed to offer a comment, 1988 is still quite sometime before the very different circumstances in Bosnia in 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that changes meant to centralise the defence forces would not necessarily have been completed by 1991?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is entirely possible, but I think I have to draw a distinction between the shifts in national strategy reflecting -- which were then reflected in organisational changes don't necessarily of themselves, within the professional part of the military -- and your quotes have drawn attention several times to the term "co-equal," that the professional military did not necessarily, by the argument that you're developing, mean that a decentralised form of command and control was accepted, even if there was a degree of decentralisation earlier and recentralisation of the way the strategy was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that the VRS when it was formed took in former Territorial Defence units which then became a part of that army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will agree with you that -- with that, but I will also comment, and an organisational chart which I've seen that we have not looked at today shows that from an early date, the VRS was formed on an organisational structure based on corps which had territorial areas of responsibility. And within those territorial areas of responsibility, everything that occurred was the responsibility of the military commander. And he always -- corps areas, it was a general, either of major-general or lieutenant-general rank, who were answerable directly to the Main Staff headed by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that the absorption of TO, Territorial Defence units and commanders, with the history of the duality of the All People's Defence doctrine that we just went through, introduced elements of decentralisation and confusion within the VRS during the early days of its formation?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think confusion is a very good word to introduce into our conversation, particularly as not all the military operations that the VRS were conducting were ones of defence, which Territorial Defence was naturally an expression of, but many of the operations were operations of offence, of moving into areas not previously controlled by Bosnian Serb forces, and, therefore, not -- there is not a direct applicability of all aspects of Territorial Defence being relevant to the activities of the VRS who, in some areas, conducted offensive operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We're at the time for the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- time for a break. Mr. Dannatt, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then before we actually take that break, Mr. Groome, the Registry informs me that it has not yet received notification that the documents we earlier talked about, that's documents covered by the 27th -- the decision on the 27th motion, 92 bis, have been uploaded into e-court. But once that has been done, the Registry will assign numbers and give the status as ordered by the Chamber this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could move along to another document, 1D1234. This is dated the 24th of March, 1994. It is a UN document sent to the Chairman of the Commission of Experts, Mr. Cherif Bassiouni. And if we could turn to page 2, we can see that it is the report on the military structure of the warring parties. Now, I'd like to turn to page 6 in e-court. And I'd like to go through some of the items here, starting with number 10: "The TDFs and, in the case of Croatian, the ZNG, are known as militias (milicija) and have a separate command structure from the regular army. Nevertheless, they join in the armed conflict, frequently operating with the regular army and under regular army officers' command. But they also operate independently in certain geographic areas, usually where most of the personnel in these units comes [sic] from." Number 11: "In addition, two other types of paramilitary groups and formations are also engaged in military operations. They consist of: (a) what is called special forces; and, (b) local police forces augmented by local armed civilians. All the warring factions make use of such forces among their combatants, but the lines of authority and the structure of command and control are confused, even to the combatants." Number 12: "There are 37 reported special forces which usually operate under the command of a named individual and with substantial apparent autonomy, except when they are integrated in the regular army's plan of action."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I would stop there and ask you, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, before you do so, I would like to know more about the -- what this document exactly is because it was sent to Mr. Bassiouni, I do understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but it comes from the administrative secretary --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and the document reads in its heading that it's the 10th draft of a certain document. Is there a final version of this document, because it seems to be very much an internal working document of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour. And I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With an unknown author.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm. The final expert report is in -- in e-court as 1D1447.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why don't we then look at the final report instead of a working document which, by its character, seems to be an unfinished product.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Because some of the language is not in the final product.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That there may be good reasons for that, but I let you go at this moment. But please be aware that this is -- that I express the concern on behalf of the Chamber for the use of this document. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I also ask for some clarification as to which period or what period, is it even a period that's within the indictment or is this a reference to the pre-indictment period.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, if we look at number 5, which would have been on page 3, it's talking about in May 1992, the JNA's FRY forces officially withdrew from Bosnia, and it's talking about the ORBAT subsequent thereto. If you could scroll down, I think that's down -- oh, there it is. So we're talking about periods that would be within the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But is that the time-frame for the -- I mean, I see that it's mentioned there. But is that the time-frame for the document as a whole or ... or I'm just trying to find ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you could assist the Chamber in finding, apart from one line which says that at a certain moment the JNA withdrew, which seems not to be in dispute, but whether that defines the time-frame for what is said in the report. Otherwise, it's still unclear to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm a little confused. We have a gentleman who is being presented as an expert witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you can answer my question, then I would appreciate that. Otherwise, we can move on. But I think Judge Moloto would have a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Ivetic, is if this is a draft and you say the final document doesn't have some of the language that is contained in it, in this draft, isn't that indicative of the fact that even the drafters of this document decided to abandon that language and therefore move away from the positions expressed by that language? And that now, we are not putting to the witness the final position of the drafters but we're putting to them something that was work in progress and which they abandoned?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to 1D1447, the third page of the same. And this -- this is the 1994 final version of the UN expert report. If we can turn to the -- I had it as the third page. Is this the third page in the document in e-court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the third page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ah. We need to go to the 31st; I apologise. I have the abbreviated version in front of me. The 31st page, if we look at paragraphs 119, 120, and 121, I think we'll find that the exact identical language is in the final report but for the change of instead of 35 special -- 37 special groups, it's now 45. So I will combine my questions to the expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you have knowledge of such a confused situation with such a large number of groups operating with apparent autonomy in the region at any point in time during the existence of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most certainly. And you touch on confusion, which is a point we've already touched on already.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can now turn to -- if we could turn to paragraph 122 which should begin on the bottom of this page of the official version. We'll stick with that. And it reads as follows: "Some towns and villages formed paramilitary units, which are not to be confused with the special forces mentioned above. These local forces operate in the areas of their towns and villages. Occasionally, they also lend support to similar groups and other combatants in the same opstina (county) and neighbouring areas. Their command and control is local, and the chain of command difficult to establish, through characteristically, these groups, like the special forces, have an identifiable leader. Frequently, the unit or group is called by the leader's name. Otherwise, the unit or group uses a politically significant name or the name of their town, village, or area. The leadership is local, mostly consisting of political figures."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you take into account the existence of such formations in terms of your expertise?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most certainly. But I would also point out to you what I have already said, that in the case of the Bosnian Serb part of Bosnia, that the VRS operated under a corps arrangement where the geographic area of the country was divided into corps tactical areas of responsibility and within those areas of responsibility, irregular and militia special forces and other armed groups came under the authority of the VRS itself. Whether they always followed that authority is another issue but they, by regulation, were under the command of the commander of that corps tactical area of responsibility. And in my experience, these groups were small and by definition incapable of carrying out large-scale military operations, such as the movement of 30.000 civilians from Srebrenica and the undoubted execution of around 8.000 of those, their burial, exhumation and reburial. That kind of activity requires a high degree of command and control and resources and is not characteristic of the kind of militias, special forces, and armed civilian groups to which you refer. I also note that much of what you refer to refers to Croatia and its development and not to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That was why I wanted the draft report that had all the 47 forces named which included Croat, Bosnian, and Serb forces. Was that part of your expertise, sir, that that there were these forces on all three of the groups that I've mentioned, the Serb side, the Bosnian side and the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Irregular forces characterised all three warring factions in that particular war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to move to a related topic. If we could take a look at your statement again, P2629, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we'll be looking at page 10 -- pardon me, page 11 in the English, page 10 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 38 of your statement. And I want to focus on the last part of this paragraph where you say: "An example of one of the groups Mladic would have been responsible for can be found on video," and then you list it and you identify it as the Skorpions video. And I want to ask you, first of all, what is the basis of your research that leads to the finding that Mladic would be responsible for the group that is depicted in the Skorpions video? What sources or documents did you consult for this?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis for my comment is founded on the overall conclusions of my research, and if the Court will forgive me for a degree of repetition, within the Bosnian Serb republic part of Bosnia, the country was divided into corps tactical areas of responsibility and all the military groups, whether VRS or irregular, were under the command of the corps commander of that area an answerable directly to the Main Staff in which the senior person was General Mladic. That is the basis of the comment that you've just drawn my attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Based upon your expert review, can you tell us from what area or municipality the Skorpions come from?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I refresh your recollection that it's Djeletovci, Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm -- I -- just point out the significance of that, would you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that, in fact, this unit was affiliated with the assistant minister of interior for the Republic of Serb Krajina, Mr. Mrgud Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll take your word for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking if your expert review uncovered that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer of the witness clearly indicates that the witness has no personal knowledge but that he has no reason to challenge what you said, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you consider yourself to be an expert with sufficient knowledge of the laws and regulations in respect to the police forces of the SFRY, the FRY, the Republika Srpska, and the Republic of Serbian Krajina, such as to be qualified to render expert opinions as to those laws?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "sufficient" is, I think, relevant. My expertise is based on a wide-ranging set of subjects and issues, and bringing those wide-ranging issues together I believe qualifies me to be of assistance to the Court, to the extent that I can at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There has been significant and detailed testimony at this trial describing of how the Skorpions unit was under the direction and control of Mr. Milovanovic as well as the Serbian State Security Police or DB. Did you have access to information of that nature at the time that you were rendering this opinion about the Skorpions that is set forth in your statement?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion with regard to the Skorpions is that if they were operational in the Bosnian Serb republic, then, by account of the explanation that I have given today two or three times, they would have been operating within one of the corps areas of responsibility that you've referred to the Krajinas. This could well be under the 1st or 2nd Krajina Corps area of responsibility, and, therefore, by the same process that I've described more than once, ultimately under the control and command of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to study the laws on resubordination of the Ministry of Interior forces to the army at the time of war, specifically the Law on Internal Affairs, provisional Law on Internal Affairs relying for the time-period of war, was that part of your research?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have looked at those documents. I can't recall the exact document now, but I am aware in general terms of the relationship between the police and the military within the context, which I've referred to several times, of the corps tactical areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that police units resubordinated to the army for purposes of combat retained their police commanders during that combat?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that during that period of combat, they were under command of the military in the tactical area of responsibility of the corps in which they were operating with its relationship that I've referred to several times to the Main Staff and to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that after combat is completed and that the police units then return to their police work they are no longer resubordinated to the army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is entirely likely. If they're no longer taking part in military operations, then their primary function is the policing of the civilian community and that is what I would expect them to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree that such an analysis of whether police forces were subordinated or not to the army at particular instances is lacking from your expert statement?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's an omission, I'm very grateful that you've brought it out in cross-examination for illumination of the Court. I think that's why I'm here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to switch to another topic. You mentioned yesterday your belief that the 2nd Military District -- at least I think you were talking about the 2nd Military District. You said a Military District was created --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So are we talking about the --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And your belief that that was created such as to become the VRS. I'd like to ask you if your research uncovered that the headquarters of that district as well as the units subordinated to the district as non-Serb personnel left, they were not replaced by anybody and thus the overall size of the headquarters and personnel in the units shrunk? Or shrank.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I mean, it was, back to this word "confusing," a confusing period and inevitably a military headquarters, any military headquarters, populated by a variety of people when there is, as happened in 1992, a parting of the ways on ethnic grounds, I think is the right way to say it, then a number of people are going to leave, to take up alternative employment or occupation within the grouping of which they have -- from their ethnic origin. This left the Bosnian Serb people a reduced number to populate that headquarters until such time it was reorganised and more were appointed to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now the VRS Main Staff headquarters was located near Han Pijesak. Did your research reveal that this location was actually the fallback or rear command post of the 2nd District and the 1st Army, rather than being a primary command post?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's where General Mladic went to exercise command when he was appointed around about the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The JNA 2nd military headquarters, when it had been situated in Sarajevo, when it had been fully staffed according to the formational rules of the JNA, would you agree with me that it had perhaps over a 100 members in this composition? Perhaps you even know the precise amount that I don't.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know the precise number. It depends which units that you count as part of the overall headquarters, whether it's just the commander and his immediate staff or whether it's the support staff, whether it's the communications staff, whether it's the local protection staff. You can answer that question in a variety of ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about what we do know, the VRS. Would you agree that the time of its formation, the Main Staff of the VRS was comprised of a total of 12 persons of whom five were generals?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the number that I've seen written down and the fact there were five generals doesn't entirely surprise me. It was to be the Main Staff and they were senior people. Some of them were already generals. Some of them got promoted quite quickly to become generals, heading up the Main Staff functions, which is what I would expect to see on the Main Staff of an army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you whether, when reading the number of 12, whether you would consider that to include support staff, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I wouldn't. My understanding of that 12 is that they were principally staff officers or immediate assistants in order to carry out the initial staff functions of the Main Staff. Undoubtedly, that number would have grown as support staff and communication staff and close-protection staff were added over time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion of what percentage of manpower the Main Staff operated under for the duration of the time-period 1992 through 1995?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, was your question to do with percentage?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Percentage of the manning of the staffing of the Main Staff. You said people were added and it grew. I would like to know what your opinion is based upon your research of how much it grew and what level it attained of its staffing as foreseen by the regulations?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can offer a view on what percentage or what numbers. It's quite clear that it grew for the reasons that I've already given. I can't give you a figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, my figure is based on Mr. Richard Butler, at transcript page 16813 of this trial, where he said the Main Staff was manned with only 37 per cent of the officers that were foreseen by the establishment. Would you agree or disagree with that figure, sir, based upon your research and expertise?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, I'm not entirely clear of the question you're asking me. Could you just -- this percentage figure? Percentage of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Officers, as foreseen by the establishment documents for the VRS.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah-ha, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was operating at 37 per cent of its --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I think what you're suggesting to me -- and I apologise if I'm drawing out the question but I can't answer a question until I understand it. I think you're suggesting that there was an establishment figure of officers and men for the Main Staff of a certain size but that it was only filled to 37 per cent?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's what Mr. Butler says, sir. And I'm asking if you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not got no reason to disagree with Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree that a proper analysis of the command structure of the VRS should take into account the officer staffing levels at all ... let me start again. Would you agree that a proper analysis of the command structure of the VRS should take into account the officer staffing levels within all units subordinated to the -- to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't particularly agree with that. I think what matters more is what the Main Staff actually achieved. How many people were in the Main Staff, actual number against their establishment, I don't think is relevant. This is an input conversation. What I'm suggesting is that the output, what the Main Staff achieved, was really rather more relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must object to this line of questioning. When I look back at Mr. Butler's testimony, I see that it was put to him the figure of 37 per cent and I just read the first line of his answer: "Well, again, yes, sir. I mean, while I don't understand -- or I don't recall the specific numbers ... I think I've testified I've never done analysis of the specific numbers ..." So it doesn't seem that Mr. Butler has offered that figure of 37 per cent or any precise number that I can find.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I see is that the page referred to is that by January 1995 that the Main Staff was only staffed at 37 per cent of the officers that were foreseen under the establishment. 41 per cent of the necessary junior officers, and 50 per cent of the necessary soldiers or it says non-officers, but perhaps it should -- we should understand it as non-commissioned officers. That is what I read on page 16813.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's the question, Your Honour. I think we need to look at the answer to see what Mr. Butler said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see. Yes, it's the question, I do agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the witness, Mr. Butler, then said indeed that he had not studied it. So it is the position of Defence that was put to you rather than the evidence, the testimony, given by Mr. Butler. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can call up document, P338.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's one that apparently you did look at. It's an analysis of the combat readiness of the VRS from 1st April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 71 in the Serbian this should be page 80 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, sir, can you advise that you in fact did review this document for purposes of your expertise?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's come up on my screen yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can get the first page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It looks familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we go again to page 80 in English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We haven't seen the first page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this does this appear to be a document that you would have --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 80 in English that will correlate to page 71 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to take a look at the last bullet point with you, which reads as follows: "In total, in the Army of RS, of the 14.541 officer establishment posts, 7.287 or 51 per cent are filled with officers, of whom 1.579 or 22 per cent are active officers, and of the 12.032 non-commissioned officer establishment posts, there are 12.942 or 108 per cent non-commissioned officers, of whom 1.190 or 8 per cent are active non-commissioned officers ..." Sir, would you agree that such a low staffing level of active officers and active -- and a low staffing level of active NCOs, or non-commissioned officers, would negatively affect the ability of the VRS command and control to function irrespective of which model is employed?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. It depends on who the additional people were, what their educational background, what their previous experience had been, and my conclusion would be that's where you have got less experienced or less well-trained people, there is a greater degree to exercise a tighter degree of control in order to ensure that the intent of the commander is carried out in the best possible manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could take a look at the next paragraph in English, which is at the top of the page in the B/C/S -- of the next page in B/C/S, I think we see the ethnic makeup of the officer corps of the VRS and we see that one quarter of the same is non-Serb: "The national structure of active officers serving in the Army of RS" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Ivetic, where are you reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's the first paragraph in English after the last bullet point. It's in the middle of the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- in e-court. Should be the top of the page in the B/C/S: "The national structure of active officers serving in the Army of RS is: 37 Montenegrins, 204 Yugoslavs, 62 Croats, 26 Macedonians, 33 Muslims, 13 Slovenes, 2.165 Serbs, 3 Albanians, 1 Bulgarian, 2 Czechs, 4 Hungarians, 3 Ruthenes, 1 Turk, 1 Jew, 1 Pole, 1 Roma, 1 Ukrainian, 21 of undeclared nationality."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree, sir, that based upon this information, the VRS did not replace non-Serb officers as a matter of policy?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with that conclusion at all. What you describe -- what is described in the document here is that the Army of Republika Srpska was indeed made up of many nationalities and different ethnic groupings. But what you don't describe is those who had formed units under headquarters of the 2nd Military District who left the 2nd Military District and went elsewhere. I find it totally unsurprising that the VRS was made up of different nationalities. And with the indulgence of the Court, I will comment that when I commanded the British Army, it was comprised of individuals from 42 different nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did those officers that left the 2nd Military District go on to join other armies and do you consider their departure to have been voluntary?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how you possibly expect that I could answer that question, to tell you where all the officers that left the 2nd Military District went to. I think we can conclude from evidence that the majority of them left to go to other factions and continued their involvement in the war in that way. And I believe that yesterday I mentioned that it was an interesting feature of the first conference that we held in the early days of the implementation of the Dayton Agreement to see the commanders of the three warring factions in the south and the west of the country greeting each other as former comrades as they had all had former service in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm a bit puzzled by the last bullet point and the following paragraph you have drawn our attention to. Because in the last bullet point, I see that there were close to 1600 active officers involved. Whereas, in the following paragraph, the active officers are represented by their ethnic or national background, but that is about approximately 2.500 active officers, so I have -- I'm puzzled by how can you give the ethnic or national background of close to 1600 officers by telling us how it was divided over the two and a half thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I invite you to read the bullet point that says that there are 1.579 active officers and that there are 1.190 active non-commissioned officers which, indeed, I believe would be the figure of the ethnic makeup which is over 2600.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I try to read it. In the bullet point you referenced to the 1190, which, by the way, would make the problem even bigger than it is, is about non-commissioned officers, you would say the active officers would include the non-commissioned officers? Because where the language "active officers" is used in the last bullet point, second line, the number of 1579 appears. The same language, "active officers," is used in the following paragraph, which amounts to some, all together I would say close to 2500 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 2500, correct. That's what [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because you -- you asked me to read it carefully. I tried to do that. I've now explained to you what my attempt of careful reading led me to -- led me to believe what was said. And the puzzle now has not been resolved for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My understanding was that it was in relation to both commissioned and non-commissioned officers. I was hoping that the expert would be able to enlighten us further and he is not been able to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that was a question that you put to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The question was not put to the witness. Mr. Ivetic, it is unsuccessful attempt to shift the blame, if there's any blame, to someone else, which is not appreciated. If you thought that it would be an explanation by adding up 1579 to 1190, then the puzzle still would be there because there is a considerable difference between that total and the total of the numbers we find in the first paragraph following the last bullet point. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, for purposes of your analysis, did you take into account the organ known as the Supreme Command which existed at all times in Republika Srpska and exercised command over the army and the defence system?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As an expert, can you please tell us how many members of the Supreme Command there are?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not going to be tested in that way. It has a composition of about six or seven members, and it was not a fixed membership. It did change over the course of the war in 1992 to 1995, but it was headed by the president, President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As an expert, can you tell us if General Ratko Mladic was ever a member of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was a moot point, and it was decided, to my mind quite correctly, that he should not be a formal member. Because -- and this gets into a very interesting philosophical debate as to what the Supreme Command represented and what the Main Staff represented. If the Court will indulge, I will try and explain that and be as brief as possible. The Supreme Command decided national, what one would call in military terms grand strategy, what the nation of Republika Srpska wanted to achieve and issued direction on that, set out, if you like, grand strategic objectives. They were then sent in a directive of one sort or another to the military command to carry out the military objectives to formulate what in doctrinal terms we would call military strategy. And that was the responsibility of the Main Staff to develop that military strategy into campaign plans at what we would call, in military terminology, the operation level of war. And that was why it was very important that General Mladic was not a member of the Supreme Council but took instructions from the Supreme Council in order to be able to carry them out by the military, the army under his command. And that separation of membership was often debated but it was felt to be more appropriate that he was not a member of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were the military court systems and the military prosecutors also separate from General Mladic's command?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's usual for the military judiciary system to stand apart from the command and control system of the military so that it retains independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move on to General Mladic's presence on the ground in Srebrenica and the Hotel Fontana that you testified about yesterday. At transcript page 19071, you talked of Mladic keeping close control and issuing directions. I wish to now take a look at part of your testimony from the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 1D1444, page 71 of the same, which should correlate to transcript page 5713 of the underlying document. If we could focus on lines 24 through 25 for the question and then we'll have to turn the page for the answer which is on lines 1 through 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I read: "Judge Riad: But there was no sign of General Mladic giving direct orders to the subordinates of General Krstic? "A. No, sir. I think we've looked at that several times previously, and I can see no evidence of General Mladic giving direct orders to constituent parts of the Drina Corps and therefore bypassing the normal corps command and control structure. I don't see any evidence of that." Do you stand by this testimony as being truthful such that you would so repeat the same today?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I don't see any evidence of that. That's not to say it didn't happen. But I don't see and didn't see any evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, yesterday we talked about Mladic leaving for meetings in Belgrade. You discuss this at paragraph 40 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is, again, P2629, MFI, it's page 12 of the same in English, page 11 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to draw your attention to the part where you say: "I am aware that in the trial of Momcilo Perisic, Carl Bildt testified that he met with Mladic and Milosevic on 14 July 1995 and Sir Rupert Smith testified that he met with Mladic and Milosevic on 15 July 1995. Mladic was therefore personally informed and involved with what was going on above him and below him. In my opinion, he was very much part of the plan and its execution." Sir, was it your understanding for purposes of this meeting that Mr. Mladic appeared of his own accord or was he requested to be present by someone?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume you're referring to the meeting between Mr. Mladic and Mr. Milosevic the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Both of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's an interesting question. I -- I can't remember whether he was requested to attend or not. But having looked at the substance of the conversation that took place particularly between Mr. Mladic and President Milosevic as recorded in Mr. Mladic's notebook, the tone of the conversation was such that he would probably have been asked to attend because the tone is critical.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now we're mixing apples and oranges. I'm talking about 14th and 15th July. You're talking about the meeting with Milosevic that occurred several weeks later.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall this meeting 15th of July as being the one that you talked about where you said General Smith, according to General Mladic's diary --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- made some comments and that your opinion was that General Mladic did not do enough as a general and seemed to not do anything and you made certain comments about that. Do you recall it now?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. And you're right, I confused in this conversation, the subsequent meeting with President Milosevic later on when he criticised, as recorded by General Mladic's notebook, his activities. But to return to the meeting which involved General Smith --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- again, in the record of that, which I've seen, General Smith raises the question of massacre, rapes, and executions with Mr. Mladic. There's no record that I've seen which says what Mr. Mladic did about it. But the point that I've endeavoured to make and I think is very important is that when a senior general, in this case representing the international community, and, of course, I mean General Smith, was to draw to the attention of one of the commanders of one of the warring factions an allegation of misconduct, he can therefore -- he must -- Mladic can no longer say that he is unaware of what might or might not have been going on. And therefore when such allegations of such significance are made, it would be extraordinary if he had not then conducted some investigation to see what had gone on. I have no idea what investigation that he did conduct. But if he did not conduct an investigation, then he was negligent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, we'll have a break in five minutes from now, so therefore ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm a little confused by your answer. I'd like to call up 65 ter 1932, which was a document that was indeed on the Prosecution's list for direct examination with you and is a memo dated 17 July 1995 from Yasushi Akashi to Mr. Annan of the UN - and I'll wait for it to come up on our screen - in reference precisely to this meeting. And I think it shows that your approach is flawed. It states as follows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, in that one question Mr. Ivetic has made two comments now with respect to the witness. I think that is improper. I think he is entitled to put questions but not his comments about what he thinks it may show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
