utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, rather than commenting on the document, you're invited to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to first introduce the document to the witness and the contents of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you can read along --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, there are better ways of doing that. You are aware of that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "Mr. Carl Bildt, Mr. Thorvald Stoltenberg and myself met in Belgrade with President Milosevic on Saturday, 15 July. I was accompanied by General Rupert Smith. Milosevic, at the request of Bildt, facilitated the presence of General Mladic at the meeting. Mladic and Smith had a long bilateral discussion. Despite their disagreement on several points, the meeting reestablished dialogue between the two generals. Informal agreement was reached in the course of the meeting on a number of points between the two generals which will, however, have to be confirmed at their meeting scheduled for 19 July. In view of the highly sensitive nature of the presence of Mladic at the meeting, it was agreed by all participants that this fact should not be mentioned at all in public." Sir, given that General Smith and General Mladic had agreed on a number of points to be confirmed at a 19 July meeting already scheduled and given the instruction to keep Mladic's presence at this meeting confidential, does this shed some new light on another reason why General Mladic didn't need to rush back to Srebrenica to investigate claims made by General Smith?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The short answer is -- is no. Your question and this document don't tell me what the number of points were. And you missed the point of how command and control works. General Mladic didn't have to rush back to Srebrenica to commence an investigation. He had merely to pick up a telephone, give an instruction to a staff officer to initiate an investigation. I don't think that your question -- well, I'm sorry, you rather lost me on the point you were trying to make and I think I have probably said that I can all usefully and unhelpfully say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your question is full of assumptions, suggestions, which need to be specified before we -- one of those questions would be whether the meeting was and what was discussed during the meeting, whether that was a reason for something still to be established, that Mr. Mladic rushed back to investigate, for example, that's -- those are all implicit assumptions, suggestions, which, without being made explicit, would not elicit answers that would assist the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page of this document, we'll see the compacts understandings agreed to and reached between General Rose -- pardon me, General Smith and General Mladic and we'll see whether they're reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you see the second paragraph here saying: "The specific agreements will be revealed after the meeting of General Mladic and General Smith scheduled for Wednesday, 19 July 1995." Would you agree that it would appear that the international negotiators requested that everyone, including Mr. Mladic, keep this under wraps?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry -- I don't -- I don't follow the question. I understood from the previous document that it had been decided for unspecified reasons to keep the presence of Mr. Mladic at that meeting secret. But forgive my stupidity, but I don't see the question that you're trying to ask me now. Perhaps you would be kind enough to explain it in great detail so I can give you answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure. Can we start reading from the top: "Understanding from Belgrade discussions, situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, 15 July 1995. General press line. Mr. Akashi at his request and in the presence of Bildt and Mr. Stoltenberg was informed of certain possible relaxations in the Bosnian Serb position. The specific agreements will be revealed" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Nobody can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "The specific agreements will be revealed after the meeting of General Mladic and General Smith, scheduled for Wednesday, 19 July 1995. "Srebrenica. Full access to the area for UNHCR and ICRC."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, we could invite the witness -- first ask him whether he is familiar with those under items "Srebrenica" or ask him to read it. There's no reason to read it aloud. And perhaps even we could take a break, if there's a hard copy of this page, so that the witness could familiarize himself with those points and you can ask any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't have a clean hard copy. I don't know if the Prosecution does. It's their document. Otherwise I could have one printed and brought up. I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, apart from the sarcasm, the Prosecution will -- Ms. Stewart will print the document for the witness. I don't keep hard copies of every document that we've disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's appreciated that either party would provide the witness during the break with a clean hard copy of this page. And we already ask the witness to leave the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the clean copy will find its way to the witness and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I hope so. I don't know how to effectuate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I hope so. I don't know how to effectuate it on my side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have it here and I'll leave it with the Registrar, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. We'll take a break and we'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I briefly address the following. The -- it is the about the Prosecution's submissions related to P1501, P1502, P1736, P1379, P1740, and P1481, made in its submissions made in the informal communication of the 31st of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll deal with all those exhibits individually after -- at a later point in time. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, have you an opportunity to review the understanding from the Belgrade discussions and in particular the points that were agreed as to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that this sheds new light on what was actually discussed at the meetings and what actions Generals Mladic and Smith agreed to, to address the concerns of General Smith from the first part of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree it's a very interesting document. At the time, General Smith only knew what General Smith knew. We now know rather more. The date of the meeting and the dates of the activities agreed are themselves interesting because by the 21st of July, 1995, when it was agreed that Generals Smith and Mladic will observe the move of the Dutch battalion out of Srebrenica, the killings and the burials would already have been complete. Therefore, there was no reason for access to Srebrenica by General Smith to be denied. Furthermore, I'm very interested by the totality of the agreements reached on that occasion, and they are quite widespread. Agreement seemed to have been reached on UNPROFOR resupply routes, troop rotations, freedom of movement agreements, and even discussion of a conference for a cessation of hostilities. These are significant events that would not have come about unless something very significant had happened. My deduction, as an expert witness and with some considerable knowledge of the circumstances, is that General Mladic conceded these points in considerable fear that the actions that had taken place around Srebrenica would play to his and the Bosnian Serb republic's disadvantage, and he made a number of concessions at that time to try and improve his position. That is my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, would you concede that another reasonable view from this same document is that a general who had just personally left with Srebrenica and had seen with his own eyes that no one was being raped and no one was being killed, would agree to the international negotiators to allow them to come in, take a look, agree to all their demands and show that he didn't have anything to hide. Isn't that another possible reading from this document, sir? And the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You know as well as I know that those who were massacred in the area of Srebrenica were buried a considerable distance away from Srebrenica and that any civilians remaining in Srebrenica would be unaware of what had happened to those who were taken away. I do not agree with your analysis at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As an expert, sir, did you examine the relevant VRS regulations to determine what the effect was of General Mladic's leaving the zone of responsibility of his army, that is to say, if his command continued or reverted to some deputy?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an interesting and moot point and gets at the heart of a relationship between a commander and his deputy commander who, under VRS regulations, is also the Chief of Staff, and, as we know was General Milovanovic. When General Mladic left the country and went to Serbia, then, in leaving the country, command devolved from him to General Milovanovic. That was the regulation. What we know from practice is that when General Milovanovic exercising authority as the authorised deputy invariably then cleared any decisions he taken with General Mladic and made sure that he was completely comfortable and up to speed with events that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender Prosecution 65 ter number 1932 as the next available Defence exhibit in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1932 receives number D410, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can return to your statement, P2629, page 19 in the English, page 16 in the B/C/S, in the middle of paragraph 56 you state that: "In accordance withstanding procedures for operational security, the commercial telephone system would not be the normal method of passing sensitive information, military orders or routine reports." Do you know if General Mladic in the vehicle that he was using to travel to Belgrade had any secure communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. And I don't think I can understand why you think I would know that. But thank you for asking the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dannatt, there's no need to express, again and again, your appreciation for what Mr. Ivetic brings to your attention. If you just answer the questions, that would --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. It's my natural courtesy, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can take a look at another topic then, the issue of reporting, I'd like to call up 1D1444 in e-court, page 81 of the same. It's, again, the Krstic transcript. And I'd like to start from line 10 and go onward through the questions and answers that were given: "Judge Riad: General Dannatt, I would still like to have some precisions" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please kindly slow down for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "Judge Riad: General Dannatt, I would still like to have some precisions, although I have understood you very clearly. You spoke about -- of the daily combat reports, and I can just quote one part of your report. You say: 'I have seen evidence of daily combat reports that are clearly in a laid-down format which provides a full account of all activity.' "Did this daily combat report give an account of the massacres? "A. No, Your Honour. I have not seen direct reports of what you would describe as massacres. As I said in an earlier answer, there were -- and I wouldn't expect to do so either, because I think most people would have realised that to commit to paper, in a formal daily report matters like that, was laying themselves open to subsequent investigation as indeed the business of this court is all about. "But one does see in some places references to things that one knows afterwards were indirect references, whether it's to prisoners, and I'm thinking now of the Zvornik Brigade's report complaining, if you like," if we can go to the next page, "of the large number of prisoners being held in schools and other reports relating subsequently to engineer equipment being moved and fuel being requested or being made available. "So I see no direct reference to what you've described, sir, as massacres, but I have seen several examples of indirect references that we now know refer in part to that process. "Judge Riad: Now, to go further, if these daily combat reports were submitted to the Higher Command, so the Higher Command was not informed about the executions if they are not mentioned in the combat reports, just to follow the echelon, how would you know about it? "A. In a direct sense, Your Honour, I agree with you, and -- I would agree with that point, sir." Do you stand by this testimony as being truthful and accurate as to these points, such that you would so testify today?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point being, if I can make the point, is that the reports were going to the higher headquarters and the reason that they were in -- in an opaque fashion was for the reasons that I gave, that to be precise and detailed would invite those reports becoming evidence at some point in the future. So although the higher headquarters, the higher command, the Main Staff, was not being informed, it offers no comment on whether the commander himself was aware of what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to take a look at another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To do, so I'd look at 1D1448 in e-court. And when we get that, I'd like page six of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That will be, again, your book -- excuse me. Again, if we can turn to page 6. That should correlate to the underlying book pages, I believe, 182 and 183. And I'd like to go through the part on the left-hand side which reads as follows: "The 5 October cease-fire brokered by Lieutenant-General Sir Rupert Smith, Michael Rose's successor, as commander of the UNPROFOR mission had brought to an end an eventful summer in which many of the Bosnian Serb army (VRS) gains of the previous two years had been dramatically swept aside. The predominantly Muslim Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina (the ARBiH, which I will refer to as the Bosniak army), together with the Croats of the HV (Croatian regular army) and HVO (Bosnian Croat army), who after their violent differences earlier in the war had joined together in the Croat-Bosnian Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, had made substantial territorial gains in September at the expense of the Serbs, who had been punished for non-compliance with UN demands by targeted NATO air-strikes and powerful artillery bombardments. These Federation operations had been conducted with careful precision and had been so overwhelming successful that I suspected, from my experience of teaching at Camberley, that professionals rather than the brave but (I suspected) moderately train the Croat and Bosnian armies had been at work. Were the NATO bombing and artillery strikes around Sarajevo, Banja Luka, and Doboj somehow part of the same well-orchestrated plan? Had the UN and even NATO been manipulated? If so, by whom? I could not help feeling that the Pentagon probably had the answer. Over the six months I was in Bosnia, I spent quite some time talking to the commanders on all three sides, and these conversations confirmed me in my view that expert campaign planning had been brought in to align the situation on the ground with the outcome that international negotiators felt they could deliver." Do you stand by these words as being truthful and accurate as to the facts that are set forth therein?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I most certainly do. But I would point out that there are a number of questions in the text as well as statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could you clarify for us one of those questions, where you ask: Had the UN and even NATO been manipulated? If so, by whom? What answer did you believe the Pentagon could offer to that question, sir?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try and keep this answer brief. By 1995, the warring factions and the international community had grown tired of the war in Bosnia, and efforts were increased to bring it to a conclusion. The failure of earlier potential peace agreements - I'm thinking of the Vance-Owen Plan, in particular - had foundered for many reasons, one of which was that the land holding between the two principal sides, the Bosnian Serb republic and the Federation, was unsatisfactory and not equal. For there to be a negotiated conclusion to this war, the land holdings had to be about 49 per cent, 51 per cent of the land mass of Bosnia. By a process which I found puzzling and which I investigated out of personal and professional curiosity, I wondered how the operations conducted by the Federation forces - that is, the Bosniaks and the Croats - during the spring and summer of 1995, had managed to be so successful that by the cessation of hostilities on the 5th of October, lo and behold, the land holdings of the two sides was about 50-50. And, therefore, on the ground, the precondition circumstances for a peace agreement had been arrived at. In my professional view, the Bosniaks and the Croats were not capable of springing together seven military operations into a co-ordinated campaign supported by air-strikes and the use of artillery to have achieved this on their own. To do this, they needed expert military assistance, and it is my belief that they received this from a contracted United States advisory company. The net result was that a situation was arrived at on the ground whereby Mr. Holbrooke was able to bring the parties together at Dayton and end the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And who is it, sir, that you believe manipulated NATO and the UN?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I speculate, but I think you know my answer that it was in the wider international community interest to end this war and the leading player in the international community by that stage was the United States. I will also add as a tail-piece that General Smith said to me on one occasion while this activity was going on, It seems rather strange that wherever the Federation forces advance, circumstances were such that he felt it was right to order air-strikes. And he wondered to me privately who was pulling the strings, and he felt that his strings were being pulled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I didn't interrupt the witness for -- I think for good reasons but, of course, speculation which was the first part of his answer is not what the Chamber assists. The second part of answer, of course, refers to facts. That is conversations the witness had with General Smith and therefore I'm glad that I didn't interrupt, although the speculations observation stands. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, General, the appraisal of General Krstic by General Mladic which we looked at yesterday, this occurred shortly after this time-period when the Bosnian Muslim and Croat armies were attacking the Serbs with the support of NATO air-strikes. Do you concede that perhaps the appraisal of General Krstic is more focussed on this event and defending the republic in the face of such overwhelming enemy forces supported by the United States?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have always paid considerable tribute to General Krstic's abilities as a military commander and I have no doubt that his conduct throughout the war from 1992 to the cessation of hostilities in October 1995 was of a very high order. That is, of course, a separate issue to the issue of any misdoings by him. I note that he was convicted of a number of offences and is in detention as a result of a sentence passed by this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you rely upon that conviction for any of the expert opinions that you have formulated for purposes of this trial, sir?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be so presumptive as to have a view that's contrary to the findings of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is not an answer to the question whether would you have different views. The question was whether you relied on those findings by the Tribunal when preparing your report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That question is not on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Consistent with an earlier answer today, when I gave evidence in the trial of the Tribunal against General Krstic, I left that hearing in my own mind convinced that he had been guilty of at least the offences relating to Srebrenica, and that was when I formed my view. That view has not changed. I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not fully, as a matter of fact. Your personal convictions about the matter is not the same as whether you used it as a basis for your report. You can ignore your own feelings in drafting a report. You can rely on your feelings which, as you explained, are related to the findings of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is fair to say that I took as fact the findings of the Tribunal and therefore it was a working assumption on my part that General Krstic was guilty of the offences as charged and therefore he had a major role to play in the massacres at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. If we could rewind to the conversation you had with General Smith that we just talked about, where you mentioned that he remarked that he felt as if his stings were being pulled. Could you give us some indication, if not a month or day, but perhaps was that still he was commander of the UNPROFOR forces?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. When I deployed to Bosnia on that occasion, it was in October 1995. General Smith was the commander of UNPROFOR, and I was the commander of Sector South-West. So he was my immediate boss, someone I had worked for on a number of occasions in the past and would count as a friend, and the conversation that I just alluded to was a private conversation between us in October or November, I can't remember exactly when, 1995, when we were reflecting on the current situation and how we had got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to complete the picture, by that time the offensives by the joint Croat-Muslim forces and the NATO air-strikes had been completed?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Dannatt, yesterday at transcript page 19109, you agreed with Mr. Ivetic that the command model employed by individual armies lies along a spectrum with the manoeuvrist approach and the centralised command approach at opposite sides of the spectrum. My question on this topic is whether you have an opinion regarding where on this spectrum the Army of Republika Srpska falls.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be short, it falls closer to the paradigm of centralised control. I think it's a point that I've made many times over the last two days, and I would do so in the context that centralised control is the effective way of controlling a disparate, largely conscript, not highly trained army and reduces risk when it comes to the translation of a commander's intent into successful operations on the battle-field.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now Mr. Ivetic has also made the point that difficulties in fully staffing officer positions may have had an impact on the command structure. In your review of General Milovanovic's evidence, did you see anything to suggest that he felt the ability to command subordinates was either compromised or diminished by not having all staff positions filled?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And in my wider experience -- and it was a point I was going to make earlier but if I may I'll make it briefly now. When we discussed an hour or two ago the different nationality and ethnic makeup of the Main Staff, I reflected on the time in my career when I commanded the Allied -- NATO Allied Rapid Reaction Corps and had officers from 17 different nations under my command, and the multinational nature of that did not reduce the effectiveness of that headquarters but there were a relatively small number of officers on who one could completely rely and others that -- let's be kind and say made up the numbers. So my point is that numbers in a headquarters don't actually dictate the effectiveness of that headquarters which was the point that I was trying to make earlier. What really matters is the output, the effectiveness of the headquarters, not the number of staff officers sitting at desks and looking at screens or talking into radios.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now again this topic you said at transcript page 36 today: "There is a greater degree to exercise a tighter degree of control in order to ensure that the intent of the commander is carried out in the best possible manner." In a situation of possible staff shortages, can you explain what you meant in more detail including at what levels of the command structure would you expect to see a tighter degree of control?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, without repeating part of my last answer, I would just say, again, that numbers in a headquarters don't have a direct bearing on the efficiency of that headquarters. The efficiency of a headquarters is more determined by the quality of the key staff officers. I'm just looking at the second part of your question to make sure that I answer it rather than run the risk of waffling.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could ask you to address this concept of tighter control in such a situation and whether that -- is that one level or did you intend that to mean more than one level of command?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the way of exercising tighter control is in part to pass more detailed orders and, in second, to require more regular and detailed reports on how the conduct of operations is going. In that way, the high headquarters is best informed, and if operations are not going in the way that the superior headquarters or superior commander requires, then further direction can be given and adjustments can be made. Now, this isn't necessarily something that is just done by radio or e-mail. The position and influence of the commander is important, and it's a common command or leadership technique that where greater supervision needs to be made, a commander will go forward to the subordinate headquarters, make a judgement for himself on how things are going, and, if appropriate, give further direction, encouragement or whatever else he feels is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now if I can change topics --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, if you would allow me one question in between. I'm a bit puzzled by the percentage discussion and the quality of those remaining. I have not heard but I'm asking you whether the functionality, if the functionality is affected, that that would have a great effect? For example, if all persons knowledgeable on communications would fall out, then the functionality, apart even if you would have 92 per cent staffing level, it wouldn't function any further. Now, first of all, I would like you to tell me whether you would agree with this thought? And, second, if so, whether you would tell us whether or not you noticed any basic functionality failures within the command structure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite clearly, if there were insufficient members of staff in any given function and that function ceased, then there would be a partial or potentially complete failure in command and control. But, Your Honour, it's very interesting, in another document that I have read, I think it was actually part of General Milovanovic's evidence, that he says that at no stage throughout the war did command and control, particularly relating to communications to enable command and control, break down except for one very short period when a number of NATO strikes destroyed a number of command installations. And I think, if I remember correctly, he said that the length of time that communications had broken down was only a matter of hours and it may have only been -- I think the number 2 hours comes to mind. So following General Milovanovic's evidence, it would appear that the main command, control and communications function of the VRS remained intact through 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just gave that as an example but perhaps the same would be true for a complete failure of transportation facilities or -- well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, military operations are characterised by things going wrong. It always happens. We call it the fog of war. If transportation collapsed, it would be a problem, it would be a nuisance. But I picked up on communications because if communications break down, you can no longer exercise control and you can't exercise command. That is an important distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it's a vital function of command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we cannot speak, we cannot communicate, I can't decide, I can't give direction, I cannot command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic spent a considerable amount of time today asking you questions about the military history of the Yugoslav army and he put a passage from Professor Gow's book to you at transcript page 18. It said: "War-time experience had shown that small units operating locally could not be centrally commanded." And this was a description of an earlier point of history in the Yugoslav army. Did you see any evidence that the VRS was comprised of small units operating locally that could not be centrally commanded?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The short answer is no. My understanding from my research is that the VRS was an organised army. It was poorly resourced at times in terms of fuel, ammunition, and equipment, but it retained a coherent structure. And in my personal experience, right through the latter days of the war and into the implementation period of the Dayton Peace Agreement, it remained a coherent organisation. That said, we were aware of militias and irregular units on all sides that played a role in the war, but that didn't characterise the nature of the VRS which -- which remained an organised being right through the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 790 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivetic pursued this line of questioning with respect to paramilitary groups and Territorial Defence groups. This particular document that you will now see before you was issued on the 12th of May, 1992, I believe. Just wait until we can see this. Now, here -- this is a document entitled: "Decision on forming the Army of the Serbian Republic of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on 12th of May, 1992." Can you draw your attention to Article 2 which states: "Former units and staffs of Territorial Defence are re-named into commands and units of the army whose organisation and formation will be established by the president of the republic." Can I ask for your comment on this article given the line of questioning Mr. Ivetic had about the -- the inability of a centralised command to control Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I come back to the answer that I gave Mr. Ivetic on a number of occasions. That, irrespective of the existence of irregular militia special forces units, the nature of organisation of Republika Srpska and the VRS was that the territory controlled by the VRS was divided into corps tactical areas of responsibility. And all those militaries, paramilitaries, and when taking part in military operations, police forces, within that area, came under the control of that corps headquarters. And, as we all know, the corps were given geographic names: 1st Krajina Corps, 2nd Krajina Corps, Drina Corps, et cetera. So that, I think, gives ample clarification of the situation and it's enshrined by Article 2 of the decision on the 12th of May that you've just redrawn my attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would tender this exhibit, 65 ter 790, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 00790 receives number P2799, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2799 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I now ask that P501 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Dannatt, I want to show you another document which may illustrate the same point with respect to paramilitaries. This is an order signed by General Mladic on the 28th of July, 1992, and is in response to some of the armed groups that Mr. Ivetic has brought to your attention. The order is signed within two months of Mladic's appointment. The first part of the order describes the problem roughly in the same terms as Mr. Ivetic has described it. Once you can orient yourself to the name of the order and the date, can I ask that we go to e-court page 2 and look at the actual text of the order issued by Mladic himself. And we see here, in paragraph 1 of this order: "All paramilitary formations and their leaders, if their intentions truly are honourable, are to place themselves in the service of the just struggle for the survival of the Serbian people and are to offer to incorporate themselves into the regular SRBiH army units, to be deployed in accordance with their military specialities and level of military training." Before I seek your comment on this, I would ask that we go to the next page, and if I could draw your attention to paragraph 7, which states: "I will hold the corps commanders in their areas of responsibility and the SRBiH army Main Staff chief of intelligence and security affairs responsible for the implementations [sic] of this order." Is this an illustration of the concept that you've just described for us in your last answer?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's more than an example. I think it's the -- it's the order, the unambiguous order that these special units must come under the corps commanders in their areas of responsibilities. I apologise for repetition, but I think I've made that point probably half a dozen times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now if I can change to a different topic. Mr. Ivetic has suggested to you today, with respect to the 15th of July, 1995, meeting, that the desire to keep Mladic's presence at that meeting confidential somehow prevented him from taking appropriate steps to investigate General Smith's claims. Based upon your experience as a senior commander, is this a plausible reason for General Mladic to have failed to have done anything in response to the report by General Smith?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I give a two-part answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question misstates the evidence and the questions that were raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please assist Mr. Groome in where you think he misrepresented the evidence so that he can correct this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe I indicated that the document showed that appropriate steps were taken. The -- the document being the document that was introduced, the 15 July understanding reached between Generals Smith and General Mladic as reported by Yasushi Akashi, another participant of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Ivetic is right, that at least in his question it was not suggested that Mr. Mladic could not take the appropriate steps to investigate. I think there was no reference to an investigation. The witness has testified about that, about what he considered to be a natural duty to investigate if that information reaches you, but it was not the suggestion Mr. Ivetic made. So would you please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, let me add one more element to my question. The agreement that Mr. Ivetic put before you, General Smith, when he was before this Chamber, was asked about this agreement and whether UNHCR ever did gain access to Srebrenica to which he replied at transcript page 7344 to 45: "I don't think UNHCR ever got access in the end to Srebrenica. "Q. Did Mladic ever give an explanation as to why they were not given access? "A. Not in my memory, no." Having the benefit of General Smith's evidence on this point, does that cause you to question the sincerity of the agreement that was entered into with General Smith on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It causes me to -- to doubt the sincerity of it, but there was a terrible track record throughout the duration of that conflict of agreements being reached at conferences that were never carried through on the ground. So as disappointing as that observation is, it is not a surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic also spent some time asking questions about matters related to General Mladic being in Belgrade during this period. Given all of the circumstances and your study of the documents and the -- the practical ways in which command function was exercised by the VRS, do you have an opinion whether or not Mladic was in command of his troops while in Belgrade on the 14th, 15th and 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the letter of the law and VRS regulations, when he was in Belgrade, he was not technically in command of the army. Command having devolved to General Milovanovic as deputy commander. But, in practice, and I have said this before, General Milovanovic would have done nothing that did he not think General Mladic would have agreed with, and any decisions that he took, he would have cleared with General Mladic at the first available opportunity. Therefore, whether, in Belgrade or in Sarajevo, General Mladic continued, in effect, to continue to exercise command over the army. And you invited an opinion, and if I can express an opinion, the lack of evidence that's come to light of General Mladic conducting an investigation into the allegations put to him by General Smith occurs because, actually, General Mladic did not need to conduct that investigation because he knew exactly what had gone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One or two in recross based upon the document that's now on the screen. With Your Honours' permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'd like to -- if you would not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to clarify the issue about the document in which the agreement was laid down. I tried to analyse the line of questioning and the answers given by the witness. I just try to summarise that and would like to hear from the parties whether my recollection is correct or not. And I invite the witness also to carefully listen to my summary. It started with a -- an observation by the witness that if you receive information about executions and rapes, that the witness considered it to be appropriate to take as a measure, to investigate. That's how it started. Then, Mr. Ivetic, you put to the witness the content of the document in which the agreements were described, which is the -- I think it's the memo sent to Mr. Annan and sent by Mr. Akashi. Then you took the witness to the relevant portion where the content of the agreements are described, and you asked the witness whether the instruction to keep Mladic's presence at the meeting confidential, or secret, whether that shed any light on another reason why General Mladic didn't need to rush back to Srebrenica, as you said, to investigate claims made by General Smith. So we are still dealing with the need to investigate. The witness then said no. And then I think the further questions were mainly about what was agreed. I got the impression, first of all, that no explanation had yet been given by the witness, so, therefore, whether there's any other explanation, it's unclear what the first explanation was. And I, in re-reading it, I gained the impression that to investigate allegations of executions and rape were then, in one way or another, linked to all kind of other matters which were agreed upon; that is, ICRC to have access, et cetera, et cetera. So, therefore, the -- both questions and answers are puzzling me. I then understood from your question, Mr. Ivetic, that -- and it was an implicit assumption, I think, in your question - that the obligation to keep matters secret and the silence in the document containing the agreements would have a direct link with the executions and rapes as they were put on the table by General Smith. First of all, is my summary of questions and answer more or less in line with your understanding of what was asked and what was answered?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Except for the last part, Your Honour, and perhaps it's because when I started reading that section you did not let me finish. The secrecy is also in relation to the agreements that were reached, including the one that is for the ICRC to have immediate access to prisoners of war, to assess welfare, register and review procedures at Bosnian Serb reception centre in accordance with the Geneva Conventions as to Srebrenica. So if a general like General Smith makes -- raises issues of -- of misconduct having occurred, and if a general like General Mladic agrees send in international agencies to assess whether everything is being done properly, that was the -- the -- the crux of the question, and the second paragraph of that understanding on the second page says that these specific agreements will be revealed after the meeting scheduled for Wednesday, 19 July 1995. So again there was an overarching cloak of secrecy over this meeting and for the agreements reached not to be revealed until that later date. That was the direction I intended to go. I apologise if I was inartful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the crux of your position. Mr. Groome, do you have any comment on my summary of what was asked and what was -- the answers were?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't think it's inaccurate. I had some other impressions, but I'm not sure it is all that relevant for me to voice them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have the following question to you. Because it comes down, to some extent, to the inclusion or the exclusion of an investigation into executions and rape in this document as part of what was agreed. If I would put you to the following, that giving access to camps, et cetera, would not in any way resolve the issue of persons being executed because they usually do not live in camps but they are buried, as you have said, already by that time, that's how I understood your testimony, therefore the content of the agreement seems not to cover the issue - at least that issue - raised by General Smith, that executions and rapes had happened. And I'm focussing primarily on executions because rape victims may still be visited by ICRC, if need be. Could you please comment on this understanding of the relation between what Mr. -- General Smith put on the table and the content of the agreement -- agreements reached.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I agree with your assessment. I see nothing in the page headed "Understandings from Belgrade discussions" that tells me that there had been any conversation, any further conversation, between General Mladic and General Smith, and between General Mladic and anybody else, that instigated any kind of investigation into the allegations that General Smith had put to General Mladic previously. And the agreement, the understanding about the ICRC having immediate access, is -- is very clear. It's -- it's fine. But they're going have access to people who were alive, who were at the Bosnian Serb reception centre. These weren't the people missing because by that stage they were dead and they were buried some distance away from Srebrenica itself. History records that, and that is fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, any further questions? I'm wondering whether -- how much time you would need because we are at a time --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would say approximately five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then would you prefer - and perhaps you want to consult with your client - to do that now? Mr. Groome, next question being whether you would wish to start with Ms. Tabeau's evidence today after a break which would leave us some 20 to 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My request would be in this session that we finish General Dannatt's testimony and that in the next session we begin Ms. Tabeau's testimony. She is waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if that is agreeable to Mr. Mladic. Because, otherwise, we would take break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My client is asking for the break at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take the break first. Could Mr. Dannatt follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While the witness is brought in, I now address some of the exhibits I referred to before the -- before. P1501, the Chamber accepts the Prosecution's position that it relates to, in addition to the testimony of witnesses with whom he has been used in court, other documentary evidence and that the Prosecution intends to rely on it in its final closing brief. Accordingly, the Chamber considers that P1501 can remain in evidence in its current form. I'll deal with the others -- I'll just continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the apologies to you, Mr. Dannatt, I just deal with a few administrative matters. As to P1739, P1740 and P1481, the Chamber accepts the Prosecution's submissions that the length of these documents cannot be meaningfully reduced without significantly undermining their potential probative value and notes that these can also remain in evidence in their present form. Turning to P1502 and P1736, the Chamber instructs the Registry to replace their current versions with the redacted ones and, in particular, with doc ID 0293-5619-RED and doc ID 0095-0901-RED. Mr. Ivetic, you still had a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My apologies again, Mr. Dannatt, for dealing with other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, I would direct your attention to the document which is still up on the screen in e-court, which is P501 which is dated the 28th of July, 1992. I would like to go through some of the provisions that were skipped and ask for your comment on the same. Beginning with paragraph number 2: "Individuals and groups which had carried out crimes, looting and other types of criminal acts are not to be included into units. They are to be disarmed, arrested, and criminal proceedings are to be instituted [sic] against them in SRBiH army courts regardless of their citizenship." In relation to that paragraph, is there anything inappropriate about a general issuing such an order as to paramilitary groups when determining whether they would be integrated into the VRS or not?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think that's a very proper exclusion of groups that he did not want to come into the military command and control structure and I take it as of -- a tacit acknowledgment that things had happened in the past that they didn't wish to happen in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you look at 3: "Paramilitary formations, groups and individuals which refuse to be placed under unified SRBiH army command are to be disarmed and arrested, in co-operation with the MUP /Ministry of Interior/ and criminal proceedings are to be initiated against them for crimes committed." The same question, sir: Would this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask for Mr. Groome. Is there any dispute about 2 and we have now 3 to be not inappropriate?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, and I'm sitting here wondering -- maybe there has been some misunderstanding but I've never suggested that anything in this order was inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I think what Mr. Groome, if I under stood him well, wanted to establish was kind of inclusion or subordination of groups, and he has not expressed in any way -- and apparently he now says that 2 and 3 are not inappropriate at all. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I direct your attention to paragraph 38 of the witness's report, which indicates: "Moreover, there is documentary evidence of General Mladic accepting command of all paramilitaries and territorial organisations," and so [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that arise from the re-examination? You could have asked this question in cross-examination, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But it is arising from Mr. Groome's dealing with this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll not stop you any further. But let's try to -- of course, all -- and that's a matter that was -- that arose a couple of times, all may be almost all or that's clear and there seems to be no dispute about these matters that where the general rule is described in paragraph 1, that some exceptions are made. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you can take the time, sir, to look through the remaining items on this page, 4, 5, and 6, I believe, and I would ask you in relation to those, is this a demonstration of General Mladic doing precisely what you as an expert would expect of a proper general to do when integrating units that had previously been labelled paramilitaries into the armed forces that one commands?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: With relation to all those paragraphs, I agree with you, that is exactly what he should be doing. It was a noble intent expressed in 1992. My query would be whether that intent was followed through in the totality of the war to 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's not the question that is put to you. And there seems -- Mr. Groome, may I take it that there is no disagreement on -- between the parties no dispute about this to be an appropriate ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, we're in a full agreement with respect to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would shortages in qualified officers have affected the ability for these orders to have been complied with at all levels down the chain?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might have affected their compliance in an immediate time-frame, but I don't see why it should have affected their compliance over an extended time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes the re-cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Groome, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: One question arising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question arising from further cross. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, what would be the implications of -- once this order is issued, of -- the period after this up until the end of the war, of paramilitary groups such as the Skorpions being incorporated into VRS military operations?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, my understanding would be that this order, as passed in 1992, had an open-ended validity and that other paramilitary groups, as might have been set up during the course of the war, should also have come under command of the main VRS structure, as was the intention behind this order issued in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, Defence, no further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: None for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then, Mr. Dannatt, I would like to thank you very much, because you're -- we have concluded your -- to hear your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. And I will remain at the disposal of the Court if I can assist at any stage in the future. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that offer. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, all that remains now is for the Prosecution to move to formally admit the expert statement of General Dannatt that's been marked for identification as P2629. And I would also tender at this time as a demonstrative exhibit, P2630, marked for identification, that's the chart that has the updated citations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would supplement our previous objection to the entry in evidence of the -- a statement as an expert report based upon the witness's concession under oath that someone else of a legal background, perhaps working for an international prosecutor's office, drafted the agreement with him. Statement, pardon me, not the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber denies your objections, including the one raised newly today, and admits into evidence P2629 and P2630. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just apart from that, just to make very clear for the record that the person who served as his legal research assistant, although she has a background in international criminal law, she has never and does not work for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I carefully listened to what Mr. -- Mr. Ivetic said for an international prosecutor's office. Not this. That's how I understood it. And apart from that, we have -- in this understanding of the additional submission, we have ruled there is no specific position that the person which may have assisted in drafting the report was specifically employed by the ICTY Office of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. And my statement was made on the witness's testimony where he said he didn't know. So I did not specify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could have further explored the matter, but you didn't, and that's the understanding of the Chamber. And we now have on the record, Mr. Groome, that you say, even if the witness doesn't know, you know where she was not employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. Then could the next witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, you'll be with us only for 15 minutes today and we'll continue tomorrow, but, nevertheless, I would like to invite you to make the solemn declaration, which is required by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Ms. Marcus. Ms. Marcus is counsel for the Prosecution, which may not come as a surprise to you. Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You provided an updated CV to the Prosecution in the past few days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that CV is uploaded and it has been now assigned the MFI exhibit number P2789. I will be tendering all the materials at the very conclusion of Dr. Tabeau's testimony as I mentioned yesterday. Your Honours, Dr. Tabeau has brought along with her hard copies of her reports for ease of reference during her testimony. I have not have had an opportunity to ask the Defence if they have any objection to her having them in front of her, but I'd like to ask the Chamber now and the Defence if that would be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As long as they're unmarked, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, you heard, as long as they are unmarked, the Chamber also has no problems. But they should be unmarked. Not even your own notes written on it, just the clean copies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, as discussed prior to the commencement of Dr. Tabeau's testimony, part of Dr. Tabeau's evidence will be tendered via Rule 92 ter and 94 bis, and some solely via Rule 94 bis. I will now lay the foundation for those transcripts and reports to be tendered via Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, did you testify before this Tribunal on the 7th of December of 2010 in the Stanisic and Simatovic case?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And in that case, did you present a proof of death, or POD, expert report dated 6th of August, 2010?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you also testify before this Tribunal in the Karadzic case on the 25th and 26th of April, and the 1st of May of 2012?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In the Karadzic case, during that testimony, did you tender an IDPs and refugees expert report from the Slobodan Milosevic case which was dated 4 April 2003?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. But actually not the whole report, just the annexes to this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Before coming to court today, did you have an opportunity to review the portions of those testimonies and the sections of those expert reports which the Prosecution is tendering now in this case?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Are there any clarifications you would like to make to that evidence at this time?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, there are no clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you confirm the truthfulness and accuracy of that evidence?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I will try my best. Your Honours, the Stanisic and Simatovic testimony is P2785, MFI. The section of the Stanisic and Simatovic POD report is P2787, MFI. The excerpt of the Karadzic testimony is -- is P2786, MFI. And the portion of the Milosevic IDPs and refugees report is 11102, MFI. Those are Dr. Tabeau's 92 ter materials. I will now move on to the attestation process for three additional items --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The number 11 --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the portion of the Milosevic IDPs and refugees report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies. That would be P2788, MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now move on to the attestation process for three additional items which Dr. Tabeau has prepared in the past few days in preparation for her testimony today. Could I ask the Court Officer to please call up 65 ter -- well, I'll give the exhibit number. P2790, MFI, which is a one-page addendum to the POD annex, P2797, MFI. This addendum pertains to four victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, was this addendum pertaining to four victims prepared by your team under your supervision in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was it prepared using the identical methodology as the POD annex?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, could you repeat the 65 ter number for P2790 MFI.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The 65 ter number, Your Honour, is 30454 and the MFI number is P2790.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you review it in detail in the same way in which the way you reviewed the POD annex prior to it being to submitted today?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you affirm the accuracy of this addendum?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I ask the Court Officer to now please call up P2791, MFI, which is 65 ter 30455. This is a table of name correspondence between the POD annex and the victims list which was attached to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, was this document prepared by your team under your supervision and reviewed comprehensively by you in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, very briefly, please, what the purpose of this document is.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: There are minor spelling differences in the names of victims in the schedules as compared with the spelling of these names in the annex to the POD report prepared for this case. This document explains the spelling differences, explains the sources which basically relate to the names as reported in the operation census and on the schedules.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you affirm the accuracy of this document?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I now ask the Court Officer to please call up P2793, MFI, which is 65 ter 30465. This is a list of corrections or clarifications to the proof of death annex, which is now given the MFI number P2797.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, did your team prepare this list of corrections and clarifications to the POD annex under your supervision in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review it comprehensively prior to coming to court?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you affirm its accuracy and the accuracy of the POD annex in conjunction with these corrections and clarifications?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the POD report, which will be P2796, MFI, contains updated numerical data emerging from this table of corrections. In other words, that report has been updated with these corrections. The Prosecution was, however, not planning to produce an updated version of the POD annex in that it is 656 pages, and this might be cumbersome. We what we were planning was, with leave of the Chamber, is just to have the POD annex kept as it is and with this table of corrections one can compare the two. This is just as we do in our practice with witness statements and we tender a clarification with it, that was the way in which we planned to proceed with the POD annex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any objection by the Defence on this way of proceeding?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to the POD annex, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may proceed as you suggest, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Finally, Dr. Tabeau, based upon your expertise, do you affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of the results of the analysis carried out in your expert reports for this case; namely, the 2013 Srebrenica update report, P2794, MFI, and its annexes, P2795, MFI; the proof of death report, P2796, MFI, and its annex, P2797, MFI; and the IDPs report for the Mladic case, P2798, MFI?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just now, in my two minutes remaining, present a very brief public summary for the witness, and I have explained the purpose of this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If can you do it in two minutes, you're invited to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Ewa Tabeau is a demographic expert and statistician whose evidence relates to the demographic shifts which occurred during the wars in the former Yugoslavia. She testifies about the process of updating the list of Srebrenica missing and the DNA-based identification of Srebrenica victims. Dr. Tabeau also provides expert evidence pertaining to the circumstances of deaths of approximately 2.000 named victims from the municipalities component of the Mladic case. Your Honours, that concludes the public summary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Marcus. Ms. Tabeau, we'll adjourn for the day. But I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, either given today, or still to be given in the following days. We'd like to see you back on -- tomorrow, at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, III. And you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 13th of November, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 13th day of November, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.15 p.m.,
